sql_threads.py:160 awaits asyncio.wrap_future(future). CPython's _chain_future propagates cancellation of the asyncio future to the concurrent future by calling source.cancel(). concurrent.futures.Future.cancel succeeds only in PENDING state and returns False when RUNNING, so a started call finishes. For a cancelled queued call, the worker's set_running_or_notify_cancel() (line 123) returns False and the call is skipped. For a running call, set_result later is ignored by the chain callback because the destination is already cancelled. The done callback (lines 143-152, registered at 162) returns early if future.cancelled() and otherwise logs after the call finishes. This matches the claim. This is from my knowledge of the stdlib; I did not read the stdlib source in this environment.

sql_threads.py:158-163: on asyncio.CancelledError, add_done_callback is registered on the concurrent Future. A running future cannot be cancelled, so it later completes via set_result/set_exception on the worker (lines 127-129), and Future invokes done callbacks on that thread; if already done, the callback runs immediately. In _log_call_after_cancel (143-152), future.cancelled() returns early before exception(), so exception() (which would raise CancelledError on a cancelled future) is never called then. When the future is done and not cancelled, exception() returns without blocking. Any callback exception is also swallowed and logged by concurrent.futures.

The defect no longer exists at head. src/sqllens/agent/integrations/sql_threads.py:65-137: there is no _idle semaphore and no get_nowait/queue.Empty path. submit (81-92) starts all SQL_WORKER_THREADS workers up front (_start_workers, 94-103), and workers block on self._work.get() (120). Concurrency is therefore bounded only by the fixed worker count, so there are no stale idle permits and no under-spawning. _busy is used only for the saturation warning, and it is updated under the lock. The worst a race can do is make one warning misfire, which is harmless. I did not search the tests, since the cause is gone from the implementation.

The visibility defect is fixed at head: sql_threads.py:112-116 _warn_saturated uses logger.warning (not debug) with worker count and queue size, rate-limited to once per SATURATION_WARNING_INTERVAL_S (60s, lines 61,109), triggered from submit when busy >= max_workers (lines 87-91). Operators at the default level now see saturation, distinguishing queueing from a slow database. The unbounded wait remains (run_blocking_sql line 160 has no timeout), but the module docstring (lines 12-14) states this deliberately ('no queue timeout'), and the harm named (no operator record) is addressed by the warning. Searched for readers of the debug message: none remain in the file.

Fixed at head: sql_threads.py:143-152 _log_call_after_cancel logs INFO 'A SQL query finished after its caller was cancelled.' when future.exception() is None, and WARNING with the exception type otherwise. It is registered in the except asyncio.CancelledError branch (lines 161-163). So a write committed by an abandoned worker leaves a breadcrumb. Module docstring (lines 29-34) documents this.

The quoted sentence is gone at head. sql_threads.py:10-16 and transport.md:115 now say a WARNING is logged when a call arrives while every worker is busy, rate-limited to once per 60s, and all workers start on first use. This matches submit (sql_threads.py:84-92): all workers start before queueing, saturated = self._busy >= self._max_workers, then _warn_saturated logs at warning level (105-116). Grep of transport.md for 'no idle'/'idle thread' found nothing. The 'pool still filling' case no longer exists since all workers start on first use. The defect was fixed.

Fixed at head: sql_threads.py submit (lines 81-92) calls self._start_workers() (line 85) before self._work.put((future, call)) (line 89), with a comment saying a failed start leaves nothing queued. If thread.start() raises (line 102), the exception propagates before the put, so no orphan item is queued. Prior evidence no longer holds.

Fixed at head. sql_threads.py:118-137 `_run` wraps the loop body in try/except BaseException with logger.exception (line 133-135) so a worker never exits; call exceptions go to future.set_exception (128-129). Workers are therefore not lost silently; the pool size stays fixed, and a failure to hand back a result is logged. The prior claim of silent permanent shrinkage and no logging no longer holds. Searched the file for other worker-exit paths: the loop is `while True` with no break/return.
Fixed at head: sql_threads.py:69-70 `if max_workers < 1: raise ValueError(...)` in _DaemonThreadPool.__init__, so zero or negative pools cannot be built and work cannot hang in the queue.
